f: Rings hands recurring fixes to Gardener and code problems to Budding
w: Patterns Rings finds overnight become Gardener skill seeds, and code problems become Branch PR requests.

Every Trunk has its own copies of the seven files; non-default Trunks start blank with one-line hints, edited in Customize › Trunks › Files, owner-only access, carried in backups, removed with the Trunk, and shown by level.
Export everything that is remembered as JSON or JSON Lines to a desktop file, and restore complete memory state from it.
On each memory write, similar current facts are checked for contradiction and closed, so answers use the fact valid at the asked time.

f: Local index of mail, calendar and messages
w: Mail (by UID cursor), CalDAV calendars and message sources are synced into a local searchable projection that returns source identifiers.

The Library holds Trunk memories and documents: attached CSVs land there and survive restart, documents open with real previews, "Made for you" and "Write a new document", versions of what Trunks make, and tabs on phone.
A map view draws topics and documents and how they connect, with "Ask the map" and compare.
A page showing the learning loop's history and its measured gains.

f: Ideas from history and personal feed
w: A personal feed of ideas drawn from history, with an editable prompt and "write like you".
An embeddable chat widget and a browser extension, both shipped off because they carry this computer's key.

f: Office documents: live cowork and operations
w: Create and edit office documents live with the agent.
One registry builds every model provider by name from config, environment variables and stored credentials, and resolves 'provider/model' strings to a ready client.
Third parties can add new model providers as plugins without changing the core.
One typed client and message model covers chat, streaming and tools across many providers, so the rest of the app never talks to a vendor SDK directly.
Dozens of hosted OpenAI-compatible and native providers (Groq, DeepSeek, Mistral, Together, Fireworks, xAI and more) are available out of the box, mostly as data rather than code.
Native support for DeepSeek, Qwen/DashScope, Zhipu GLM, Moonshot Kimi, Doubao, MiniMax, Baidu Qianfan/Wenxin, iFlytek Spark, ModelScope and Xiaomi MiMo.
Native Anthropic Messages API with thinking blocks, signatures, tool_use pairing and prompt-cache breakpoints, including Anthropic-compatible endpoints.

f: OpenAI and OpenAI-compatible provider (Chat Completions and Responses)
w: Calls OpenAI and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint through Chat Completions or the Responses API, keeping reasoning items and call ids across turns.
Streams Responses API calls over a pooled WebSocket to cut per-request latency.

f: Google Gemini and Vertex AI providers
w: Gemini API and Vertex AI with native message and tool conversion, thinking settings, Google Search grounding and GCP auth.
Bedrock Converse (and SageMaker endpoints) with the AWS credential chain, profiles, regions and cross-region inference profiles.

f: Azure OpenAI and Azure AI Foundry providers
w: Azure OpenAI deployments and Azure AI Foundry with API keys or Entra ID keyless auth.
OpenRouter models with their metadata, caching, attribution and provider-routing preferences (cheapest, fastest, only listed companies, fallbacks).
Native Ollama: discovers and pulls local models, streams NDJSON, keeps models warm and handles tool calls.
Hosted Ollama Cloud models with an API key and a merged live catalog.
Finds LM Studio's loaded models, loads them on demand and maps reasoning effort to what each model allows.
Connects vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp server, LocalAI, TGI, MindIE, Atomic Chat and other local OpenAI-compatible servers as providers.
Discovers Anaconda AI Navigator/Desktop and syncs its locally served models into a provider.

f: Local endpoint discovery and setup detection
w: On setup, probes installed CLIs, local model servers and saved credentials to offer what already works.
Users define their own OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible providers with base URL, key, headers and model list.
Routes requests through a LiteLLM proxy so one gateway handles 100+ providers and virtual keys.
Databricks model serving with OAuth/PAT auth and gateway routes.
Snowflake Cortex models with Snowflake's message and tool format.
Hugging Face inference endpoints after a Hugging Face sign-in.
Meta's model API using short-lived keys minted from a Meta identity sign-in.
Uses subscription coding plans (Kimi Code, GLM, MiniMax, Bailian, Volcengine/BytePlus Ark) as model providers, with endpoint auto-detection.

f: Hosted model gateway as a provider
w: Sign in to a vendor's hosted gateway (credits-billed, many models behind one key) and use it as a model choice.
Server-side OpenAI-compatible gateway that resolves model aliases to primary and fallback upstreams, rotates upstream keys and hot-reloads routing.
Sign in with a ChatGPT Plus/Pro account by browser PKCE or device code and run Codex models on the subscription through the ChatGPT Responses backend.
Sign in to a Claude subscription by pasting a setup-token or via a PKCE OAuth loopback flow, stored as a refreshable credential.
One pluggable login registry lists every subscription product (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Kimi, xAI...) and its auth methods behind a single login command.
Imports or reuses Claude Code, Codex, Qwen and desktop-app credentials already on the machine instead of a new sign-in.

f: Claude Code CLI as a model backend
w: Runs turns through the installed Claude Code CLI (stream-json or PTY) on the owner's Claude subscription, with the app's own tools and approvals.

f: Codex CLI as a model backend
w: Uses the Codex CLI (codex exec per turn) as a model provider, with the chosen model passed on each call.

f: Gemini CLI as a model backend
w: Uses the gemini CLI as a provider with session resume.

f: Cursor Agent CLI as a model backend
w: Uses the cursor-agent CLI as a provider after checking its auth.
Pick Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot or other ACP agents as the runtime, installed from a pinned registry, with model switching mid-conversation.
Parses a user-typed ACP launch command into argv safely, without shell quoting.
Each signed-in account's CLI credentials (Codex auth.json, Claude folder) are materialised into their own private home so accounts never mix.

f: Agent CLI sign-in status and identity probe
w: Runs CLI status commands (e.g. claude auth status --json, codex login status) to tell 'connected' from 'ready' and show the signed-in identity.
Device-flow GitHub sign-in (incl. Enterprise), Copilot token exchange and Copilot model calls.

f: VS Code Language Model API provider
w: Uses models exposed through VS Code's LM API (e.g. Copilot) as a provider.
Login with Google (browser or user code), Code Assist onboarding and tiers, ADC and Gemini CLI OAuth reuse.
Use Grok via an xAI account OAuth (device code) or SuperGrok subscription instead of an API key.

f: Other vendor OAuth logins (Qwen, MiniMax, Oracle)
w: OAuth sign-in for Qwen, MiniMax and Oracle Code Assist with runtime credentials.

f: OAuth flow that mints an API key
w: One-click browser flows (OpenRouter, Requesty, Hicap, Tetrate) that create and store an API key for the user.

f: Shared OAuth device-code and PKCE helpers
w: One set of RFC 8628 device-code, loopback-PKCE and browser-open helpers, with a desktop UI for showing codes.

f: Own cloud account sign-in by device code
w: Links a local install to the app's own cloud account with a device code (and QR) that the user approves in the browser.

f: Own cloud account sign-in by browser
w: Signs in to the app's own cloud account through a browser loopback or deep-link callback.
Users in several organisations switch the active org for billing and remote config.
API keys and OAuth tokens live in the OS keychain or an encrypted file, with file/keyring/auto/ephemeral modes and legacy migration.

f: OAuth token refresh with cross-process locking
w: Refreshes OAuth tokens before expiry and on 401, once per credential even when several processes need it, and signs out only on permanent failures.
A refresh hook fetches a rotated key on an auth error and retries the call.
Sign-out removes credentials from every store and revokes tokens server-side.
Several accounts per provider form a pool that rotates on 429/402/auth failures using fill-first, round-robin or least-used, with cooldowns and duplicate merging.
One provider holds several API keys (primary plus fallbacks) and rotates on rate limits.
A rate limit or unsupported model only benches that credential for that model, leaving it usable for others.

f: Continue on another account after a plan limit
w: When an account hits its limit mid-task, the work moves to a healthy sibling account and resumes with its context.
The model asks for a capability; code chooses the eligible connected account by policy and health.
Credentials resolve per agent, app, skill or user by routing rules, so each agent or person can use its own model account.
Borrowed secrets are fingerprinted, and single-use OAuth refresh grants are never duplicated across copied profiles.
Records which credential path (API key or OAuth) each request used, without storing secrets.

f: Subscription plan usage windows per account
w: Reads each account's 5-hour, weekly and per-model limits and reset times from the provider (headers or usage endpoints) and shows them per account.

f: /usage command with history and limit resets
w: A /usage view shows account usage, history and plan bars, and can spend a limit-reset credit.

f: Client-side request pacing near rate limits
w: Paces requests per model (FIFO admission, token bucket, shared rate-limit state) so the app slows down instead of hitting 429s.
When quota or credits run out, offers to retry, switch to a fallback model, use credits or open the provider's billing/upgrade page.

f: Account credit balance and low-balance notice
w: Shows the account's credit balance and usage, with a low/critical top-up nudge.
Server-side per-user credit balance, metered LLM/TTS/STT debits and scheduled auto-refill.
Stripe Checkout for credits and subscriptions with verified webhooks and idempotent claims.
Verifies StoreKit 2 transactions and App Store server notifications.
Pays HTTP 402 x402 payment requirements for metered cloud calls.
Terminal screens to read and change hosted-plan spending settings.
Plan selection, onboarding, limit errors and org restrictions for a vendor's paid plan.
Each reply records input, output, cache-write, cache-read and reasoning tokens and prices them into message and session cost.
Per-model prices (including cache rates), fetched live where possible and overridable for private models.
Charts token use and cost by model, user and time, with a personal usage view.
Keeps metrics per LLM role (agent, condenser, title) inside a conversation.
Counts tokens with provider or custom tokenizers and estimates usage when providers don't report it.
Shows how much of the context window the conversation uses, broken down by part, with colour thresholds.
Shows tokens per second during generation.
Blocks or warns when spend in a window (per user, org, session or task) exceeds a budget.
One catalogue of models with context limits, modalities, tool/reasoning support and pricing (models.dev, llm-info, model bank).
A bundled model catalogue refreshes from a remote source with TTL/ETag caching, so new models appear without an app release.
Fetches each provider's /models list (with caching, size caps and validation) for pickers and setup.

f: Context window and output limit resolution
w: Resolves each model's real context and output limits per route and plan, and clamps requests to fit.
Config can override a model's context size, capabilities, canonical name or catalog entries.
Per-model and per-family defaults for edit format, temperature, prompt prefixes and reminders.
Developer tool that diffs bundled model metadata against LiteLLM's.
Recommended, verified and free model flags shown in onboarding and pickers.
/model or a switcher changes model or provider in a live conversation, keeping history, with sticky persistence and auto-revert of agent picks.
A searchable model menu grouped by provider with tags, showing the model and account, in the composer and CLI.
Star, pin or recall recent models for one-click selection.
Short names (sonnet, opus, 4o) and user-defined aliases map to full model ids, optionally with provider and base URL.
With no explicit choice, picks a default model or profile from what is configured.
Asks before switching to an expensive model.
Requires confirmation for cheap tiers whose vendor trains on prompts.
One-time prompt to move to a newer recommended model.
Pick the request priority tier (standard, priority, flex) or a fast mode per model.
Warns when the selected model is not recommended for agentic use.
The agent knows which model, provider and endpoint it is running on and can say so.
Save any number of named model setups (provider, model, keys, parameters) and switch between them.
A key and base URL are stored once and referenced by many model profiles.
Each mode (plan, act, build, fast) remembers its own model or model pack.
Reusable agent profiles bundle the agent kind, model profile and options.
Each agent, workspace or user has its own default model, and each conversation can pin one.

f: Custom models wrapping a base model
w: A named model wraps a base model with its own prompt, parameters, knowledge and tools, with fallback when the base is gone.
Configured models declare roles (chat, edit, autocomplete, embed, summarize, subagent, vision...) and each role resolves separately.
A separate model (and coordinate space) handles screen grounding for computer use.
Cheap side jobs (titles, summaries, compression, extraction) go to a smaller model through an auto chain.
A separate model and edit format apply an architect's plan.
A tool forwards the conversation to a stronger, separately configured model for a second opinion.
Virtual arena models route to a random configured model so users rate answers blind.
A decision-model role evaluates evidence against a rubric and returns a typed choice, score or probability.
A classifier (rules, small model or local model) rates each request and sends easy work to a quick model and hard work to the best.
User-defined router profiles list candidate models with descriptions; the router picks one per task.
Per-slot policy chooses local or cloud models, with soft cloud fallback when local can't serve.
Individual actions resolve their own model class separately from the planner.
Strips unsupported modalities for text-only models and routes image requests to a vision model.
A built-in tool lets the agent switch itself to another saved model profile.
When the primary model fails, an ordered fallback chain is walked with cooldowns, visible notices and restore of the primary.
Configures provider-native fallbacks (e.g. Anthropic fallbacks beta).
Transient errors (408/409/429/5xx) retry with jittered exponential backoff and honour Retry-After.
Classifies provider errors (auth, billing, rate limit, plan limit, overload, context overflow, format) into typed failover reasons.
Missing, expired or invalid credentials become plain, actionable messages like 'Sign in again'.
Provider content-filter blocks become a clear error the agent can report.
A hard timeout bounds each call and an idle timeout aborts streams that stop producing chunks.

f: Reasoning effort and thinking budget controls
w: One effort scale (none to max) and thinking budgets map onto each provider's native controls, offering only the levels a model supports.
Provider reasoning is shown separately from the answer and stripped from history.
Provider-specific reasoning fields (DeepSeek reasoning_content, Gemini thought signatures, MiniMax/StepFun/MiMo) are replayed across turns.
Places cache breakpoints and cache keys per provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Bedrock, Gemini, Vertex) to maximise cache hits.
Background 1-token pings keep the provider cache warm on long tasks.

f: Provider tool and output schema compatibility
w: Rewrites tool and output JSON schemas per provider (OpenAI strict, Gemini, Moonshot, Cerebras) so calls aren't rejected.
Normalises message histories per provider (tool-call ids, empty parts, tool-result images, R1 format).
A rule table adds per-provider request options (caching, headers, verbosity, quirks).
Repairs and validates a model's JSON output against a schema without a second model pass.
For models without native tool calling, tools are described in the prompt and text-shaped calls are parsed and run.

f: Lean tool set for local models
w: Local models get a reduced tool set without high-latency or channel-dependent tools.
Installs and supervises llama.cpp (in-process or llama-server router), picks a preset from hardware and serves GGUF models.
Runs MLX models on Apple Silicon as a local provider.
llama.cpp on mobile through one Capacitor adapter.
Probes CPU/GPU/VRAM and classifies the device to recommend local model size and flags.

f: Model hub search and resumable download
w: Search Hugging Face for GGUF/MLX models, check compatibility and download with progress, pause and resume.
Reports whether the network is metered before big model downloads.
Installs OVMS and its models for local inference on Intel hardware.
Downloads a SHA-256 pinned runtime binary and manages a local model server via setup/start/stop.
Run, stop, remove and verify installed local models, activate one, and clear model caches.
Starts local model services on demand, keeps them alive with leases and readiness probes, and loads models with progress.

f: Context fit sizing for local models
w: Sizes a local model's context to the RAM/VRAM budget and asks before raising it.
Saves a thread's KV cache across sessions and spills cold pages to RAM or disk for long contexts.
One owner of all local model handles with a GPU memory budget and priority load queue.
Research-grade quantization (PolarQuant, QJL, TurboQuant) and custom GGUF emission.
Feeds image parts to local vision-capable models.
Import existing GGUF or MLX files, reading GGUF metadata for compatibility.
Uses Apple's on-device Foundation Models as a provider where available.
Uses Chrome's on-device Prompt API (Gemini Nano) through an OpenAI-compatible adapter.

f: Models on a remote GPU node
w: Exposes Ollama models running on a paired GPU host to the agent.

f: Local model proxy for other apps
w: Runs a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint so other programs (e.g. Claude Code) use the app's models and subscriptions.

f: Personal API keys for the app's API
w: Users mint scoped API keys to call the app's own OpenAI-compatible API.
Each user supplies their own provider keys (encrypted, optional expiry) or browser-side connections.
A settings page per provider for keys, base URL, model list, options and logos.
A step-by-step dialog or command picks a provider and auth method (sign-in or key) and saves it.
Add, list, order and remove accounts per provider, with per-provider credential status.
Send a tiny real request to check a provider configuration before use.
Decides whether a provider has its required credentials and is reachable before use.

f: Provider sign-in over an HTTP API
w: Web and desktop clients start and complete provider OAuth through server endpoints.
Asking in chat to add another AI account shows an in-chat block that starts that sign-in.

f: HTTP client with mTLS, proxy and OS trust
w: Shared LLM HTTP client with client certificates, proxy env, NO_PROXY and the OS certificate store.
Extra headers, body passthrough, session ids and app attribution are added to model requests.
Rewrites model ids and prefixes for gateways that name models differently.
Records which model a router or proxy actually served and shows it.

f: Scripted test models and provider recordings
w: Scripted fake LLMs and recorded provider sessions for testing without live calls.

f: API key sign-in from environment, flags or prompt
w: Provider keys come from env vars, $VAR references, CLI flags or a login prompt, validated before use.
Installs a provider's SDK package on demand or gives a friendly install hint.
Adjusts default providers and mirrors by detected region.
Embeddings from OpenAI-compatible, Gemini, Voyage, Cohere, Jina, Ollama or local ONNX models, addressed like chat models.
Reranking-role models (Voyage, Cohere, Jina or an LLM) rescore retrieval candidates.
Supports OpenAI/Azure Assistants with threads, files and tools.
Per-model and per-chat parameter panels (temperature, top-p, max tokens, seed, stop).
Submits many independent requests to a provider batch API at reduced price.
Trusted plugins get host-owned completion and structured-output calls.
Exposes which managed tool capabilities a subscription unlocks.

f: Gateway wire selection for Claude models
w: Chooses which wire protocol carries Claude models through a gateway.
Keeps a session bound to the selected ChatGPT workspace/residency backend.
Remembers the original model when a task enters the account's reserve model and offers to return.
Opts eligible accounts into a vendor model access program.
IDE or SDK clients supply subscription tokens without the app owning the login.
Registers an agent identity whose signed tokens authenticate backend calls.

f: Personal access token and workload identity auth
w: Personal access tokens and workload-identity token exchange for CI.
A provider's auth runs an external command to mint bearer tokens.
Providers declare gateway OAuth; the app runs it and stores rotated credentials.
A CLI for provider-backed model, image, audio, TTS, web and embedding calls.
Choose a cloud or fully local backend, saved or overridden per run.

f: Model settings from a remote workspace
w: Pulls the saved model profile, secrets and MCP config from a remote agent server.
Provider config is kept locally and merged with server-synced rows.
Fetches experiment flags from the backend once per session for feature gating.

f: Add a hosted-hub model by name
w: A --model owner/package flag adds a model from a hosted hub for the session.
OIDC/OAuth sign-in for any identity provider with role and group mapping, token refresh and back-channel logout.
SAML sign-in for enterprise identity providers.
LDAP bind and search sign-in with group sync.
Google, GitHub, Discord, Facebook, Apple and Steam sign-in with linked accounts.
Local email/password auth with JWT sessions.
Admins invite users; registration checks invite tokens.
Only allowed email domains may register or sign in.
New accounts verify their email, with rate-limited resend.
Password reset flows and recovery codes with rate limits.
Users delete their account and data.
Upload and crop a profile avatar.
TOTP 2FA with QR setup and backup codes.
Reuses or exchanges identity-provider tokens for downstream calls and app sessions.
Signs users in from reverse-proxy identity headers.
SCIM 2.0 endpoints provision users and groups.
Throttles sign-in attempts with a sliding window.
One-time sign-in code or link by email with rate limits.
Issues temporary tokens for passwordless login from external systems.
Skips authentication for a private self-hosted install.

f: Guest identity promoted to an account
w: A free anonymous identity lets new users start, then upgrades to a real account keeping their data.
Assign users to workspaces.
Per-user request and indexed-data limits differ by plan.
A device keypair signs requests to a free remote service.
Authenticates a Teams bot with a secret, certificate or managed identity.
MTProto user-account login with OTP and 2FA.
X sign-in with PKCE and refresh-race-safe token storage.
GitHub device-flow login bound to the agent that started it.
Each helper (delegate, fan-out, specialist) gets its own model and exact account, kept through continuation and restart, settable in the window, or inherited from its Trunk.
Each Trunk picks its own account per provider (shown by email), can copy the owner's accounts, and follows its own rotation and limit rules.

Branch's own Accounts page and 3-step Add-an-account dialog: service groups, quick names, Trunk chips, ordering, answer first, rename, sign out, bulk select, retired services, aliases and hidden owner emails.

f: Usage ring and 'What each connection has left' popover
w: The protected usage ring at bottom right and its popover: fixed heading and buttons, scrolling subscriptions, exact local reset times and the status-bar line.

f: Checkpoint offer near a plan limit
w: Near 95% of a plan, offer to save progress so Trunks checkpoint.
Models settings tabs (Connections, Defaults, On this computer, Second opinion, Media), the four default slots and Advanced readout rows.
No fake model, sample answers or practice mode; with no model, a plain refusal pointing to setup, and the old BRANCH_PROVIDER=demo route removed.
First run 'How should Branch think?' (shown once) and 'Connect your accounts', each row really signing in, showing emails, and a first real task within two minutes.
Connect a keepoak.com account and decide whether a customer's ChatGPT plan may run on a KeepOak-hosted computer.
Test the model you use, or compare models side by side on your own test suites.

f: Codex app-server as a model backend
w: Run Codex through its app-server: Branch tools via thread/start dynamicTools and item/tool/call, models/account/plan windows from model/list and account/rateLimits/read, and resume, steer and interrupt for hand-offs.

Claude transport specifics from the Hermes DirectSDK plugin: model list and plan type from the initialize reply, [1m] routes, an idle (not fixed) deadline, the cacheHistory body-rewrite A/B test, and crediting the plugin in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.
Optional request-level cache that returns a stored answer for an identical request (ships off).
Stream structured (schema-shaped) outputs as they generate.
Ask several models once per user turn and merge the best, or let two models debate with a cost ceiling and a verdict.
Most steps per task, sub-tasks at once, model rounds per step, tool timeout, largest tool answer kept whole, and grouping independent tool calls into fewer rounds.
Owner/admins get commands in chats; everyone else only help and whoami, failing closed.
Scale desktop screenshots to a known size and map clicks back.
A bubble the size of its words.
Dedicated code generation and improvement tools.
The model starts child agents (helpers) with their own context, tools, model and limits, waits for or resumes them, and can list, steer or kill them.
Helpers run detached while the parent keeps working, are tracked in a background task registry, notify on finish and can be resumed after a restart.
The parent lists running helpers, sends them follow-ups, interrupts or closes one while the others keep going.
A helper can start as a fork of the current conversation, inheriting its context and tool preference.
An ephemeral fork for a quick side question that returns to the main thread and is discarded.

f: Helper depth, concurrency and runtime limits
w: Max depth, max helpers at once, per-run totals and max runtime bound the helper tree; extra fan-out in one reply is trimmed; children can only narrow tool access.
When the worker cap is hit, spawns wait in a priority-FIFO queue with starvation aging instead of failing.
Many independent helper items run from a durable store with live/running limits, leases, retries and restart recovery.

f: Delegation ledger and agent tree records
w: Every delegation and parent/child edge is recorded so later turns and restarts see which helpers finished, failed or were cancelled.
Delegations carry deterministic checks (file exists, non-empty, valid JSON) or a result schema, and a failing result is reported as unresolved.
Every tool result gets a receipt; helper reports and replies that claim a tool ran or quote a result are cross-checked against the receipts, and unbacked claims are marked.
A helper's result is delivered back to the requester (as an inbound message or announce) with retries, and a relay decides whether it goes straight to the user or to the planner.
The parent ends its turn while children work, and a successor turn starts once their completions are batched.
When a helper dies, a planner-ready failure turn is synthesized so the user hears what happened.
Silent helpers are prodded once with a status question and runaway loops or spend caps raise warnings.
In-flight helper tasks are summarized per chat only when their status changed.
When a person posts while helpers run, each helper gets the message as interrupt, queue, deliver or ignore through its own inbox.
Round-trip and respawn caps stop agents (or two bots) from replying to each other forever.
One coding request splits into independent lanes with exclusive scopes, supervised as a wave.
Helpers ask the parent to use its actions and connectors, with a capped self-spend allowance and approval for paid or mutating calls.
A parent grants a child a credential scope, collected from the owner and encrypted under the scope key.
The planner sees active helpers, their readiness, cap pressure and which coding backends are installed, to decide spawn, reuse or wait.
Screenshots and artifacts from a finished helper are posted to the originating chat as media.
Helper session events are exposed through one coordinator contract shared by API, chat and websocket consumers.
One action creates, controls, cancels and inspects coding helper tasks, workspaces and issues.
Ships general-purpose, explore (read-only codebase search), plan, execute and bash helpers.
A helper that answers questions about the app itself from its bundled docs.
Local and remote helpers share one session protocol so their runs are driven and observed like the main agent.

f: Helper approvals routed to the parent
w: Each helper's tool calls are tracked separately and its approval requests reach the lead's view, so one human approves for the whole tree.
Each helper's model comes from its definition, the parent or the catalog, pinned to available models.
Background helpers get memorable generated names.
A helper's startup prompt is estimated and capped before sending.
Each helper runs as a headless child process whose stream output is parsed, detecting lost output or crashes.
Helpers show as live cards (status, steps, token use) above the conversation and in a running-agents strip; any one opens view-only in its own panel.
A message can spawn a thread for helper work, shown in a side panel.
A sub-agent that reviews or guards work without asking for approvals and forwards its events to the parent.
The agent consults a stronger model profile for advice on hard decisions.
A thinking level that adds plan, execute, verify guidance and fans work out to helpers.
Named agents defined in markdown or TOML (model, tools, skills, MCP servers, permissions, budget, hooks) from user, project and extension folders, with a registry that reloads them.
New or changed project-level agents must be acknowledged before they register.
Describe an agent and a builder agent writes its prompt, model, tools and skills; the agent can also create and update other agents.
A panel to build and edit agents (instructions, model, tools, files) with version history and duplicate, plus management pages and an /agents command.
Agents carry uploaded avatars shown in lists and messages.

f: Several agents with their own workspaces and routing
w: Several agents run side by side, each with its own workspace, auth, memory and sessions, and each inbound message is routed to one by channel, account, peer or group bindings, with a default for unbound chats.
A default agent is created at startup and answers whenever no agent is chosen.
Each chat-app DM user automatically gets an isolated agent with its own workspace and history.
Changing persona, model or tools for one chat makes a private agent tied to that conversation.
Files chosen for an agent become its own knowledge that its chats search.
Agents are private, protected or public, enforced for visibility and knowledge access.
A browsable gallery of shared agents with categories, search and one-click install.
An agent's identity, workspace files, skills, plugins, MCP servers and routines package into a versioned file that installs, migrates or exports.
Installed agent packages update with a capability-change summary and roll back on failure.
An agent package installs its declared schedules and MCP servers and removes only what it owns.
Create a coordinator plus researcher, writer and reviewer from role templates.
Agents are listed as @mentions in the composer and a message starting with @name hands the turn to that agent.
The current agent, user, session and task travel with the work so tools write to the right place.
Shared team workspaces with links, and approved transfer of resource ownership.
Agents hand a conversation to another agent through handoff edges or transfer_to tools, shown in the transcript.
Collaboration patterns (handoffs, sub-agents, chains) are chosen as sections in the agent builder.
Agents run one after another, each passing its output on.
A supervisor agent coordinates helpers and can process their streams, monitor sessions and message them.
A routing agent picks the next agent, workflow or tool over several iterations until a completion check passes.
An orchestrator mode with no tools splits a request into subtasks, hands each to the best mode with full context, pauses the parent and resumes it with the child's result.
Code, Plan (may only edit plan files), Debug, Ask and Orchestrator modes, plus custom modes.
Plan mode runs a planner conversation that writes a plan; Build switches to execute it.
The agent starts independent child or sibling sessions (locally or in the cloud) recorded under the parent.
A lead spawns named teammates that share a task list, exchange messages through mailboxes, auto-claim tasks, and persist for resume.
Teams attach fragments to outcomes, review and finalize them as deliverables.
An agent synchronously delegates to a teammate in its own workspace, bounded by allowed targets, depth and time, including across processes.
Teammates run in their own tmux or iTerm2 panes.
A board view of team task progress with a lane per member.
The agent writes a sandboxed script that dispatches helpers sequentially, in parallel or as pipelines and swarms, with budgets and stall detection.
Each helper dispatch is journaled so a re-run replays cached results for the unchanged prefix.
One agent messages another agent's session and optionally waits for the reply, rate-limited and policy-governed, including across local sessions.
An agent lists, prompts, stops and answers other sessions and starts new worktree sessions.
Fuzzy search of models available to sessions, grouped by provider and variant.
A board parent and child agents (or any agents) post to and read, shown as a swarm view with avatars.
A supervisor process keeps agent sessions running so terminals attach, detach and re-attach.
Many independent sessions run side by side, each in its own git worktree with its own model, across one or several projects.
One prompt runs in parallel worktrees across chosen models; diffs are compared and a winner applied.
Each configured review agent runs in its own worker and worktree with live progress.
Start and stream cloud agent tasks for a repo and branch from the CLI or IDE.

f: External agents over ACP as helpers
w: Any Agent Client Protocol agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Copilot, Droid and more) runs as a helper or provider, locally or in a remote sandbox.
External coding-agent CLIs run as first-class agents with transcript import, quota sampling and delegation from the app.
Claude Code (CLI or Agent SDK) runs as a team agent with its stream translated into messages and tools.

f: Codex as a helper (exec and app-server)
w: Codex CLI exec and app-server run as team agents, normalizing patches for the diff view.
Cursor's CLI or SDK agent runs as a team agent.
OpenCode runs as a team agent with its todo states mapped.
The Pi coding agent runs as a team agent.
Kimi Code CLI runs as a team agent.
Sourcegraph Amp runs as a team agent.
xAI Grok Build runs as a team agent.
Tencent CodeBuddy CLI runs as a team agent.
Qoder CLI runs as a team agent.
OpenAI Agents SDK agents run inside the app.
ACP sessions have lifecycle, cancellation, turn timeouts and backend failover.
When an ACP agent lost its session, or a conversation moves to another agent, history is replayed as a budgeted, redacted transcript.
The app is exposed over ACP to VS Code, Zed and JetBrains with sessions, content blocks, a model picker, slash commands and auth advertising.
Dangerous-command and edit approvals reach the editor's permission prompts, with session-scoped edit auto-approval.
Agents are callable from outside through OpenAI-compatible chat and Responses endpoints, with tools lent by the calling client.
The app serves an Agent Card and A2A 1.0 JSON-RPC (send, stream, get, list, cancel tasks, push config) so other agents can call it, with task records keyed by caller.
The agent discovers, calls, reads history from and orchestrates remote A2A agents, which also join rooms.
Remote A2A agents authenticate with API keys, HTTP auth, OAuth2 (discovered from the card) or cloud credentials.
A2A task metadata and the workspace persist to object storage with path-safe ids.
The A2A server loads settings per workspace and enforces workspace trust before running.
Long-lived workspace agents work shared threads, booked under a lock and exposed through A2A operations.
An agent is exposed peer-to-peer with no open ports so another client drives it through a relay, bridged to local ACP sessions.

f: Peer connection cards and address book
w: A shareable card with QR code carries a node's public key and address; an address book keeps known peers.
Agents message teammates on the same install, a peer gateway or another connected machine and get the reply back.
Machine-readable reason codes travel with errors so UIs can explain failed agent-to-agent deliveries.
A queued, claimed, terminal record hands a message to an agent chat exactly once.
Each bot's chat gets a roster section describing its teammates.
Each agent profile gets its own headless desktop, viewable and drivable from the app.
Several agents chat together; a supervisor (a small model) decides who speaks next or runs them in parallel.
A gateway hosts rooms with an append-only event log and a deterministic policy choosing the next bot turn, with checkpoints so busy rooms do not replay the log.
Bots on other gateways join a hosted room with scoped grants, and room authority can move between gateways via replicas.
Plugins react when room members act.
Several agents each answer the same group message in their own session, chosen by mention, with bounded follow-up rounds.

f: Multi-bot coordination in a chat-app group
w: Several bots in one Discord server coordinate replies through shared rows (speaker slots, leases, receipts).

f: Humans and models in shared channels
w: Slack-like channels with threads, reactions, DMs, member management and @model mentions, with membership enforced on history.
The model reads channels it has access to through search and view tools.
Bounded shared-room evaluations across independent agents record every delivery and reaction.
Inline widgets show orchestrator task pipelines and room views.
A durable board of tasks, runs, comments and assignees shared across agents and profiles, with idempotent create and one atomic claimant per task.
Separate boards per project with a current board pointer.
A singleton dispatcher promotes ready cards, claims them and spawns worker agents per assignee, advancing on heartbeat and schedule ticks.

f: Board worker crash and stuck-work recovery
w: Crashed, stale or orphaned workers are detected, their cards reclaimed, max runtime enforced, respawn circuit-broken and stuck cards promoted or reassigned.
Max in-progress cards come from system memory with per-profile caps and backoff under pressure.
Workers and orchestrators show, create, claim, comment, complete, block, attach proof and request review on cards through tools.
Workers hand cards to reviewers who send them back with requested changes; results are synthesized on completion.
A worker's turn must end with a terminal board action so cards are always handed off.
A card can run its worker in a goal loop with a turn budget.
A triage card is fanned out into a graph of child cards from the agent roster, or tightened into a concrete title and body.
Child cards stay waiting until parents finish; promotion is audited and reopening a parent invalidates children.
A planning root, parallel workers and a join review are written into the board.
Cards that declare a PR are accepted only when its head commit passes checks.
Each card gets a scratch dir or fresh git worktree, set up and cleaned up safely.
Chats and agents subscribe to card events and get notifications and artifacts with a replay-safe cursor.
Board list, create, show, move, dispatch, watch, gc and repair from the CLI and a chat slash command.
A whole board moves between machines as an archive.
Each card reports structured distress signals with suggested fix actions.
A kanban view of agent cards across columns with filters, card details, live steps, comments and inline approvals.
Card mutations and worker events fire plugin hooks.
Blocked cards carry a block kind, and repeated same-reason blocks go back to triage.
Each worker's log rotates by size and generations.
All agents' sessions grouped into editable columns by state and a small-model classification.
Card state stays in step with linked session runs, recovering missed events after restart.
Card changes trigger a debounced run of the board's linked automation.
Workers attach proof (command, URL, artifact) and small files to cards for later workers.
Separate queue lanes for main, nested, scheduled and helper work with capacity groups so parallel agents never deadlock.
A planner turns a request into a dependency graph of subtasks, runs ready ones concurrently on assigned devices and edits the graph as results arrive.
Newly ready tasks wait while the planner edits the graph, preventing races.
Add, remove and update tasks and dependencies through MCP tools and a command editor with undo and redo.
Devices register their capabilities, tasks queue per device, and pending tasks cancel on disconnect.
A message protocol for device registration, heartbeats, commands and tasks over WebSocket with binary frames and pluggable middleware.
Backoff reconnection, heartbeat monitoring and timeouts keep device links alive.
A typed event bus with observers for agent output, graph view and UI streaming.
A small dependency-injection container wires orchestration parts for tests.
A host agent picks the app window and an app agent per app executes the subtask.
Extra agents (hardware, Linux, a computer-use model) register with their own prompts and state machines.
A WebSocket hub routes events between the character, bots, games and plugins with delivery policies and liveness.
The main character dispatches tasks to sub-modules such as a game agent.
A multi-turn agent builds, tests and repairs workflows from chat while driving a debug browser.
After a run, a model checks each stated completion criterion against evidence before claiming success.
The agent asks a question or pauses when a credential is missing and resumes on reply.
Repeated identical tool calls and oscillation are detected and interrupted.
Code blocks are synthesized from exploration runs, linted and preflighted.
Proposed changes show as pending cards the user accepts or rejects.
Progress renders as a narrative with checklists, working status and queued messages.

Exactly one default Trunk ships (setup's first, or made quietly by the engine), chosen in Customize › Trunks from a recorded choice, keeping the owner's full memory and tools, with its own face in the welcome and empty states, proven in the installed app.

f: Unrouted chats go to the default Trunk
w: Choose who answers a new conversation; every unrouted chat (window, phone, chat apps) goes to the default Trunk, one continuous thread per outside chat listed under its Trunk; /new starts a linked new segment; loose conversations move under the default Trunk in one audited transaction.
Each household person gets their own default Trunk, files and threads; switching profile never moves the owner's fallback.

The protected Add a Trunk studio, job templates, naming before creation, an intro message, rename, pause and resume (one or all) with plain words, remove with a list of what goes, and a right-click menu.
Colour, photo, shape, eyes, motion or an emoji face; the editor shows only what the chosen face uses; helper faces are never the mascot; KeepOak personas and faces.
Which computers a Trunk may use, how many tasks at once and which it starts on.
Each Trunk has its own inbox, email, handle and face, and a live line under its name.
Routines a Trunk owns, and teaching a Trunk by doing a job once while it watches (see automation's recording and Trunk-owned routine rows).
A Trunk that fixes failed updates with its own memory, SOUL and account.

Make a room from two or more Trunks (or by dragging one onto another), with answer rules, typing indicators, room lanes, a room menu, real titles, export, Branch from here, a new group-chat dialog for 2 to 6 Trunks plus people and remote agents, and the listed room fixes.

f: Helpers out of Recent and search
w: Helper conversations never show in Recent or search.
A live overview of every Trunk, helper, computer, board and task with steer, stop and pause.

Orchard's Seed, Growing, Ripe, Picked and Blocked columns, drag a card onto a Trunk, an idempotent migration from Automations › Board that never auto-starts cards, ship-on, and a parity table vs Hermes Kanban.
Hand-offs between team members are offered, accepted, rejected or time out; the owner stays responsible until accepted, and agents acknowledge messages and claims.
Teams of small groups, each with its own lead, in Customize › Specialists.
Several specialist agents debate a question.
Requests and follow-up tasks are routed to the matching project.
Collaboration events are published under a member identity, and modified events fail verification.
End-to-end encrypted messaging between agents and people.
Rooms on Nostr relays where agents and people share threads, with a mobile push gateway.
A reviewer checks work while it happens, plus /grill to stress-test a plan.

Graph and workflow requests that the automation area's workflow rows cover (typed graphs, conditional branching, nested graphs, flow APIs, pipeline-as-tool, flow search, time travel and procedure checks).

Generic tool, execution and approval requests (code execution, sandbox, process management, tool-call inspection, toolsets, user-defined and deferred tools, ToolCallingAgent, approvals, install requests).
Agent-computer interface, vision page understanding and a long-lived Windows desktop helper.

Research pipeline (research), file editing and LSP (coding), adapter system (models), API/WebSocket gateway and gateway runtime (integrations, ops), rich message handling (chat), document processing (tools), interop leftovers, OpenTelemetry names (ops), one message box (ui), specialist regression cases (evals), widgets, waiting line, focus view, standing instructions for a specialist.
Exports traces, metrics and logs over OTLP (HTTP/gRPC) to any collector the owner names, configured by config or OTEL_* env vars.
Model calls and tool runs carry OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic-convention attributes, with streamed chunks merged and optional prompt/response content capture.

f: Typed agent run spans (agent, model, tool)
w: Every agent run, model generation, tool call and workflow step becomes a typed span with parent/child context, so a run reads as one trace tree.
Continues upstream W3C trace context into the engine and stamps one trace id on requests, runs and logs so everything for a task can be joined.
Optional OpenTelemetry instrumentation of the HTTP server, database, cache and outbound HTTP clients.
Counters, timers and gauges for sessions, tokens, cost, tool use and pool sizes with name/tag validation and buffering before an exporter starts.
A local /metrics endpoint renders engine diagnostics (RPC, queues, memory, event loop, GC) in Prometheus text format.
Tracks exporter success/failure transitions and reports exporter health as a diagnostic.
Scripts/compose files start a local OTel collector with Jaeger or Tempo/Prometheus/Grafana for viewing telemetry.
Sampling strategies and span processors decide which traces and spans are exported.
One event bus routes tracing, logging, metrics and feedback events to every configured exporter, including local storage and console exporters.
Owner configures which tracing exporters are active from the app instead of editing files.
Sends agent, model, tool and subagent observations to Langfuse with session/user correlation; optional fan-out to several destinations.
Exports traces (and metrics) to LangSmith.
Traces agent steps, LLM calls and tool runs to Laminar when its key is set; no-op otherwise.
Exports traces to Braintrust with thread reconstruction.
Exports traces and metrics to Datadog LLM Observability.
Exports OpenInference traces to Arize or Phoenix.
Exports OpenInference traces to Arthur.
Exports LLM traces and usage to PostHog LLM analytics.
Exports AI spans to Sentry performance tracing.
Exports traces to Confident AI for evaluation.
Initialises Monocle OpenTelemetry tracing once when enabled.
Wraps sessions, turns, LLM attempts and tool runs in NeMo Relay scopes for relay tracing and shared metrics.
Imports historical Langfuse traces with manifests and validation.
Stores traces, spans and metrics in ClickHouse at scale.
Persists every run as a structured timeline of steps, model calls, tool calls, usage, errors and outcome, exportable as JSON/JSONL; recording is opt-in in production.
Replays a captured run bundle step by step for inspection, analysis or restart.
Records real sessions/traffic to JSONL and replays them through a fake provider for golden end-to-end tests.

f: Share a trajectory to Hugging Face
w: Uploads a session transcript re-emitted as Claude Code JSONL so the HF Agent Trace Viewer renders it.
A trace list with filters, span tree, timeline, token usage and payload views for past runs, backed by a local trace store.
Watch an agent run step by step as it happens, with phase drill-down and raw event payloads.
Typed lifecycle, model, tool and connector events published per run so UIs, sockets and observers can subscribe live.
Renders thoughts, actions, results, diffs and task DAGs as coloured terminal panels, decoupled from agent logic.
Turns a finished run into a shareable report with each step's screenshot, action and thought, or a markdown summary.
Optionally writes every model request and response (with cost and latency) to files per session for debugging.
A console view of each model request's prompt, options, streamed result and token usage.
Hosts install a hook that sees every provider request/response and its usage, for pipeline logging and accounting wrappers.
Stores upstream request ids on assistant messages for support and debugging.

f: Token and cost accounting per call
w: Each model call records input/output/reasoning/cache tokens and a cost priced from a versioned model price table, rolled up per run, session and account.
Normalises each provider's cache-hit token fields and fingerprints the cacheable prefix so cache use is reported (unknown stays unknown).
Sums cost across a task and all its child tasks so the parent shows total spend.
A local tokenizer estimates usage when a provider returns none.
Shows tokens, tokens/sec and duration under each response or in a message details dialog.
/stats, /usage or a usage panel shows the session's tokens (incl. cached), cost, per-model/per-tool stats and budget.
Shows tokens used against the context window (and cost) in the header/status bar.
Shows how the context is split between system prompt, memory, tools and messages, from a redacted inspector or an offline prompt-size build.
Pulls plan usage, quota windows and remaining credit from provider endpoints (Claude, Codex, Gemini, OpenRouter).
Charts token and cost usage by day, model, session or agent with a heatmap and drill-down, from a local usage store.
A command/API summarises N days of tokens, cost, tools and models per project, written on request.
Exports usage and monitoring records as downloadable files.
Messages, model calls, tool calls, sessions and errors per bot/pipeline with traffic charts and CPU/uptime.
Elo leaderboard of models computed from user ratings.

f: Structured logger with levels and subsystems
w: Per-module/subsystem loggers with levels (env override), coloured console output for humans and JSON lines for machines.
Writes logs (agent, errors, gateway) to bounded, rotating/daily files with size caps, including a scrubbed startup log.
Deletes logs and monitoring records older than the retention window on startup and on a timer.
Ships logs in batches to an HTTP endpoint or Redis.
A debug mode writes namespaced debug logs to a file so the TUI stays clean.
Turns on targeted debug logging for one subsystem without global debug.

f: Secret redaction in logs and exports
w: Masks API keys, tokens, passwords, PEM blocks and JSON secrets in logs, streams and anything exported.
`logs` tails and follows the engine's structured log file with level/session filters and a local fallback.

f: Live log console in the app
w: The app shows a live, paged log console with levels and download.
/logs returns recent log lines in chat; log level can be changed per room.
A metadata-only ledger of who did what: runs, tool decisions, messages and resource changes, queryable and viewable.
Logs API requests at metadata/request/response level to a file.
Uploads prompts and artifacts to blob storage for auditing.
Captures uncaught errors and lifecycle failures, writes them locally and (opt-in) reports them to an error tracker such as Sentry.

f: Report a problem / feedback with logs
w: Owner sends a note with redacted logs and diagnostics, or opens a prefilled GitHub issue with version and OS info.
Builds a shareable redacted bundle (config, log tails, stability data) for bug reports, as a file or paste link.
Prints a paste-ready summary of version, model/provider, gateway state, paths and config.
Shows effective settings with their sources and masked secrets, plus debug subcommands for agents, LSP and skills.
Renders the assembled system prompt, message list, tools and model identity a run would send.
Opens a SQL shell on the app database or runs a query.

f: Runtime errors surfaced to agent and owner
w: Recent runtime failures are fed to the agent and repeated errors escalate to the owner, with a policy for which diagnostics reach chats.
/warnings lists startup and runtime warnings and per-plugin errors instead of losing them in scroll.
Reduces failures to a small privacy-safe kind used by UI and reliability dashboards.
Unhandled errors return an id that matches the log line; validation errors are sanitised.
Maps API and agent-server errors to localised, actionable toasts.
Rate a reply up or down (with comment); feedback is listed, aggregated and optionally sent to a tracing backend as a score.
One status field set (model, provider, approvals, tokens, context, session) shared by CLI, chat apps and TUI.
`status` summarises install, auth, gateway service, channels and tasks; `--all` adds a pasteable diagnosis.
/healthz, /readyz and /startupz report liveness and readiness of databases and channels.
Derives content-free service and cron health from runtime state for export.
Probes each backend/plugin runtime periodically and shows status dots or badges with the last error.
Lists MCP servers, LSP servers, channels and plugins with live connection and token state.
`/doctor` checks provider, model, extensions and environment and feeds repair hints back.
Batch-tests models or runs one diagnostic turn through the pipeline for connectivity and latency.
Runs an investigation of a described symptom in the current conversation.
PID, lock and marker files tell other processes whether the engine runs and in what state.
A bounded stability buffer, unclean-exit ledger and shutdown snapshot record what the engine was doing for post-incident review.
Records per-attempt stream counters and exception chains when a streamed reply dies.
Classifies stalled or orphaned sessions and releases lanes or aborts no-progress runs.
Records each scheduled run's outcome so schedules can be audited.
Watches the event loop for stalls and logs/warns when lag passes a threshold.

f: Blocking I/O detection in async code
w: Static and runtime detectors flag blocking I/O on the event loop, run in CI.
Samples CPU, memory, swap and disk and shows them in a debug bar or status API.
Warns when the data volume is nearly full; nodes report disk space.
Opt-in CPU profiles, heap sampling and heap snapshots for bug reports.
Measures CPU/wall time per startup phase and writes a timeline artifact.
FPS/lag overlays, render profiler, flicker detection and 3D renderer diagnostics.
A devtools hub with network/console inspector, WebSocket, plugin host, state-action and context-flow pages.
A movable overlay shows engine vitals, lane tables and an event log.
Developer harness server with commands to create test tasks and expire tokens.
Web dashboard, world viewer and MCP REPL for a Minecraft agent.
Opt-in benchmarks for checkpoints, concurrency, sandboxes and event-store scaling.
Detects user activity/idle periods to drive activity-based behaviour.
A local capture proxy or CDP recorder saves traffic (HAR) for debugging.
Records the browser viewport to video and cuts per-run clips as artifacts.
Screenshots, HTML, model requests and downloads are stored as artifacts on local or cloud storage.
Artifact URLs are HMAC-signed and verified on fetch.
Nothing is sent unless the owner opts in: one resolver combines saved consent, env opt-outs and DO_NOT_TRACK; asks once.
Anonymous usage events (PostHog, Clearcut, OpenPanel, custom endpoints) with a device id and an off switch.
A bounded queue-and-drain sink batches sanitised events to PostHog, an HTTP endpoint or a proxy.
Events are frozen allowlisted scalars; paths, arguments and message content are stripped.

f: Local copy of every analytics event
w: Writes every analytics event to a local JSONL file so the owner can see what was sent.
Autocomplete/chat/edit/tool events recorded against versioned schemas for analysis.
Captures sessions for a data programme, scrubs secrets and uploads in chunks.
Product and account feature flags fetched from a flag service.
Emits session/task/step events to a cloud dashboard.
Proxies browser RUM data to a configured backend.
Background git reads after replies emit a snapshot only when git fields change.
Middlewares that rewrite a tool result record what they changed so observers can tell raw from visible.
Contributors register self-knowledge summaries the agent can read about itself.
Analyses UI evidence frames and certifies test runs into signed evidence bundles.
Records each inbound platform event's routing, runner and API calls as one trace.
Gathers GitHub stars and package downloads for homepage badges.

f: Signed receipt chain with 'Record intact' check
w: Inbox › History keeps a hash-chained log of signed tool receipts; 'Check the record' verifies nothing was deleted or rewritten, distinguishes successful receipts from failed/blocked events and rejects forged ones.
Rings gates gain maxAgeDays, log-scaled frequency and pruning of the candidate table.
Progress comes from real task records: working, waiting for you, waiting for a service, blocked, each with a reason and last update; no invented percentages.

f: Workflow graph builder and run graph
w: Visual graph builder for task chains.
Proposal/approval UI for persisted plans and a structured todo tracker.
Turns data into interactive charts in replies.
One interface installs, starts, stops and queries the background engine on every OS service backend.
The engine installs as a per-user Task Scheduler task at logon (no admin), with RestartOnFailure and a Startup-folder fallback.
Under Task Scheduler the engine runs inside a Job Object owned by a supervisor so children die with it.
Writes the LaunchAgent plist transactionally and bootstraps, starts, stops and reports the engine.
Installs a systemd unit with watchdog directives and enables user linger for headless hosts.
Tells systemd when the engine is ready and pings the watchdog.
Kills any process left in the unit's cgroup after the engine exits.

f: Service definition drift audit and repair
w: Audits installed service definitions against the expected command and environment and repairs duplicates or legacy units.
Restart works when the engine runs under a custom supervisor.
A state-dir lock (plus port bind) guarantees one engine per owner/state dir; stale owners are reclaimed.
A second launch focuses the existing window instead of starting another runtime.
The desktop shell spawns and supervises the engine as a separate process so the window never freezes.
One background engine per computer hosts sessions for every client (desktop, CLI, IDE, chat apps); clients attach and detach.
start/stop/restart/status commands manage the background engine with a PID file.
A local-only socket answers versioned verbs (identify, status) so liveness is proven by a connection.
Invoke any engine RPC or HTTP route from the command line for scripting.
Child runtimes exit when their parent dies; dead or zombie PIDs are treated as stopped.
Out-of-loop watchdogs detect a frozen event loop, deadlocked startup or hung shutdown, dump stacks and force a restart.
Logs RSS over time, sheds cached transcripts under memory pressure and restarts cleanly when memory stays too high.
Tracks restarts across lifetimes, warns on restart storms and skips auto-resume when the engine keeps crashing.
Loud-but-survivable handlers for unhandled rejections/exceptions so one failing job cannot kill the engine.
Configuration failures exit with EX_CONFIG (78) so supervisors don't restart-loop.
Raises open-file limits and heap size for long-running services.
Engine, API and TUI processes set recognisable OS process names.
Detects host sleep or process freezes and restarts channels; listens to OS suspend/resume events.
Prepare an atomic host-suspension lease so the engine pauses and resumes cleanly.
While a turn runs, the computer is kept from idle sleep (IOKit, systemd-inhibit, Windows).
Periodically checks each connected chat account for stale transport and restarts it.
Notifies once when a session has pending input but its agent made no progress for too long.
Idle, unsubscribed conversations unload from memory and reload on demand.
Detects idleness and suspends the machine or reclaims idle cloud workers.
Pauses background autocomplete when on battery.
A requested restart stops admitting new work and waits for active turns and background writes; the waiting work is named and can be cancelled.
Before restarting the engine writes a sentinel; on boot it resumes pending continuations and restores sessions.
Pending inbound messages, transcripts and deferred deliveries are spooled/drained before shutdown.
Handles Ctrl-C/SIGTERM (including Electron quit on Windows) to shut down cleanly.
Clients ping/pong the engine and reconnect, rejoining threads, if it drops or restarts.
Hosts install a restart handler at startup so the agent can restart itself; requests fail loudly if unsupported.

f: Runtime introspection and control from chat
w: The agent reports runtime status and applies owner-authorised settings, provider and routing changes, then hot-reloads.
Classifies a state change into a reload tier (hot, restart services, full restart) and applies it.
A TTL lease decides which instance owns a conversation; stale leases are released on startup.
The updater stages the candidate privately, rehearses it against snapshots of real data while the old version runs, swaps only if it passes, and rolls back automatically.
The engine checks for new versions at start and daily, then installs them only when no work is admitted or in flight.
On launch the app checks for a newer version, notifies, and updates itself automatically unless the owner turned it off.
`update` detects how the app was installed (npm, bun, brew, binary) and upgrades in place, printing old and new versions.
Fetches and fast-forwards a source checkout with autostash, dependency install and restart.
Per-install channel choice resolves promoted releases per channel.
Checks at most daily for a newer release and shows a passive notice or settings card.
`update --check/--plan` reports what would update and how each runtime would restart, without changing anything.
Downloads are verified by publisher signature/provenance (Sigstore SLSA), not only a checksum.
Checks GitHub releases or update feeds and downloads/installs desktop updates with staging and channels.
One package carries old and new bundles; a cached cohort decides which activates.
Updates install into an immutable versioned folder and hand activation over, keeping the previous one for rollback.
After an update every engine is restarted, checked to run the new version, and a receipt is written; stale survivors are escalated.
Only one update runs at a time across CLI and desktop updaters.
A failed update writes a local report, stays on the current version and offers diagnose/report.
Retires recovery copies and backups after a verified update.
When git is broken, downloads a release ZIP and swaps it in with two-phase commit.
Pauses or cold-starts the Windows engine around an update and releases file holders.
After an update: migrate config with backup/rollback, verify or restore the state DB, sync bundled skills, one shared completion tail.
The updater writes stage progress to a status file the desktop renders.
Escape hatches let an old installed updater hand off to the new one so old versions always reach the newest.
Managed (Docker/Nix) installs refuse self-update with the right command; wrong-install and broken-source updates are refused.
Detects when a running engine or server is older/newer than the client and asks for a restart or update.
Shows what's new after the version changes.
CI produces nightly, preview and stable releases, patch releases and published images.
Scripts keep versions, pins and lockfiles in sync and check published versions match tags.
Generates an SBOM, publishes scoped packages and shards the test suite.
Blocks releasing commits pushed after approval or merged without passing checks.
Diffs the lockfile against the last release, looks up new packages in OSV, pins OS snapshots.
CI runs the test suite on Linux, Windows (and macOS) across runtime versions for every PR.
CI builds and smoke-tests the desktop app on macOS, Windows and Linux runners.
Tests prove upgrades keep data compatible and the installed update runs.
Repo-backed scenario runners with live transports exercise real flows end to end.
E2E suites run the real engine against a mock model or fake provider; UI dev runs against mocks.
